Thomas.strategy: Wheat with legume cover crop in fallow
Thomas.why_suggested: Replaces vulnerable bare fallow with a living multi-species or legume cover crop to build soil organic matter, fix biological nitrogen, and maximize continuous ground cover.

evidence.signal: Directly addresses the 4-month NDVI bare-field window, sustaining ground cover across summer months
Root-zone soil wetness (0.384) requires careful termination timing to avoid moisture penalty

benefits: Superior living armor against High Plains wind erosion
Biological nitrogen fixation reduces synthetic fertilizer costs
Accelerates soil organic carbon and infiltration capacity
information_gaps: Field-scale cover crop transpiration vs. fallow evaporation trade-off not resolved by satellite
Cover crop seed mix availability and cost in Northwest Kansas
risks_needing_local_review: Risk of depleting stored soil moisture needed for subsequent cash crop stand establishment
Cover crop termination timing must be managed aggressively before soil moisture is exhausted
Requires additional seed investment with no direct harvestable cash grain revenue

Thomas.why_suggested: Shortens the vulnerable summer bare-fallow window and introduces a heat-tolerant C4 grain crop to capture late-summer radiation and stabilize farm income.

evidence.signal: Sorghum vegetative canopy occupies July–September, eliminating the post-wheat NDVI bare-field dip below 0.20
C4 grain sorghum maintains photosynthetic efficiency during the 33.9 extreme heat days (Tmax >= 35°C)
Long dry spells (65 days maximum) handled via sorghum's waxy leaf cuticle and drought-induced dormancy

benefits: Durable, erect stalk residue provides strong armor against spring wind erosion
Breaks monoculture winter annual grassy weed cycles (cheatgrass, jointed goatgrass)
Produces 2 grain crops in 3 years with modest additional capital requirements
information_gaps: Local elevator milo basis and regional delivery distance not accounted for
Subsoil moisture depletion impact on subsequent wheat stand emergence requires local probing
risks_needing_local_review: Stored root-zone moisture must be at least 3 to 4 feet deep at June planting
Herbicide carryover restrictions between winter wheat and summer sorghum

Thomas.why_suggested: Utilizes deep-rooting sunflower to scavenge subsoil water and residual nitrogen below the wheat root zone, providing a high-value cash alternative.

evidence.signal: Deep taproot reaches subsoil moisture down to 6 feet during extended dry periods (max 65 days)
186 frost-free days easily accommodate 90-110 day confection or oilseed maturity varieties

benefits: Excellent deep-profile nutrient scavenging and break of cereal diseases
High profit potential under favorable oilseed crushing contract pricing
Tolerant of high midsummer daytime temperatures
information_gaps: Regional processor contracting and logistics within 100 miles of Colby
High-resolution bird predation risk maps not integrated
risks_needing_local_review: Sunflower leaves fragile residue that breaks down rapidly, leaving soil bare by late winter
Heavy subsoil moisture extraction can dry out subsoil before subsequent wheat planting

Thomas.why_suggested: Traditional baseline practice in Thomas County, relying on a 14-month fallow to accumulate subsoil moisture for winter wheat.

evidence.signal: NDVI remains below 0.20 for 6 months (Jan, Feb, Jul, Aug, Sep, Dec)
Annual heat stress averages 33.9 days above 35°C during the bare summer fallow window
Root-zone soil wetness averages 0.384 during fallow

benefits: Lowest equipment and operational input costs
Proven familiarity across Western Kansas wheat producers
Allows weed control via tillage or non-selective herbicides
information_gaps: Field-scale soil moisture retention efficiency is not measured by coarse satellite sensors
Impact of localized stubble height on boundary-layer evaporation is unmodeled
risks_needing_local_review: Severe wind erosion during dry, windy spring months (March–May)
Precipitation storage efficiency during summer fallow is often under 20%
Low soil organic carbon accumulation over multi-year cycles

Finney.why_suggested: A 3-year limited-irrigation rotation that allocates groundwater strategically to corn while letting drought-hardy wheat and sorghum thrive on partial irrigation.

evidence.signal: Reduces seasonal pumping volume by ~30%, preserving groundwater buffer for critical heat days (42.3 days >= 35°C)
evidence.source: NASA POWER Daily & K-State Irrigation Trials

evidence.signal: Wheat and sorghum stagger vegetative peaks across May and August, eliminating midsummer well strain

benefits: Saves 25% to 35% of total irrigation water, extending well life and complying with LEMA caps
Continuous heavy residue from sorghum and wheat protects soil armor year-round
Spreads labor, planting, and harvesting across spring, summer, and autumn
information_gaps: Transitioning pivot nozzles from full corn capacity to variable-rate split application
Local feedlot and elevator pricing spreads between corn and sorghum
risks_needing_local_review: Requires careful pivot management to split water across different crops under one circle
Lower gross revenue per acre compared to bumper corn crops in wet years

Finney.why_suggested: Rotates irrigated corn with a legume to reduce peak seasonal pumping overlap, supply biological nitrogen, and break corn rootworm cycles.

evidence.signal: Soybean peak water demand shifts timing relative to corn, moderating peak well discharge during heat waves (42.3 days >35°C)
201 frost-free days provide ample window for Group 3 and Group 4 soybean maturities

benefits: Biological nitrogen fixation provides 30 to 45 lbs N/acre credit to the subsequent corn crop
Completely breaks Western Corn Rootworm larval feeding cycle
Diversifies commodity price risk between feed grain and oilseeds
information_gaps: Regional iron deficiency chlorosis (IDC) risk on high-pH caliche soils requires local soil testing
Varietal tolerance to spider mites in hot, dry High Plains late summers
risks_needing_local_review: Soybean residue breaks down rapidly after harvest, leaving soil vulnerable to winter/spring wind erosion
Soybeans are highly sensitive to late-summer heat and moisture stress during pod fill

Finney.why_suggested: Existing intensive management system maximizing short-term grain volume under center-pivot irrigation, but facing severe Ogallala depletion.

evidence.signal: Peak irrigation occurs during July–August with 42.3 days above 35°C driving atmospheric evaporative demand to maximum
Rainfall variability (CV = 0.24) leaves crop entirely dependent on unsustainable groundwater pumping

benefits: High gross revenue potential in years with favorable grain market prices
Heavy corn stover residue protects against winter wind erosion
Established local grain delivery infrastructure, feedlots, and ethanol plants
information_gaps: Local well pumping capacity (gallons per minute) varies field-by-field and is unmeasured by satellites
Exact LEMA multi-year allocation balance must be confirmed with Groundwater Management District
risks_needing_local_review: Ogallala aquifer decline and impending legal water pumping limits under GMD/LEMA rules
Escalating energy pumping costs with deeper well lifts
Severe corn rootworm, spider mite, and goss's wilt pressure in continuous monoculture
